title: "Maximum likelihood"

Under the provisional Bernoulli model for BOUN accusative labels, which value of the shared probability $p$ makes the observed token sequence most probable? **Maximum likelihood estimation** answers this question by holding the data fixed and varying $p$.

The product below relies on the [independence factorization](../foundations/independence.qmd), which turns the probability of the joint observed event into a product of token-level probabilities. The [outcomes-and-events chapter](../foundations/possibilities-and-events.qmd) supplies the underlying distinction between a realized sequence and the set of sequences the model could have generated.

The same formula will play two roles. At fixed $p$, it distributes probability over possible samples; at the observed sample, it becomes a function of the candidate value $p$. We will make that change of viewpoint explicit, derive the maximizing value, and then calculate it for the BOUN labels before returning to the assumptions of the working model.

## Probability and likelihood

For one observation,

$$
p(x_i\mid p)=p^{x_i}(1-p)^{1-x_i}.
$$

Conditional independence gives the probability of an ordered sample:

$$
\begin{aligned}
p(\mathbf x\mid p)
&=\prod_{i=1}^n p^{x_i}(1-p)^{1-x_i}\\
&=p^k(1-p)^{n-k},
\end{aligned}
$$

where $k=\sum_i x_i$. As a probability distribution, this expression varies over possible data at fixed $p$. As a likelihood,

$$
L(p;\mathbf x)=p^k(1-p)^{n-k},
$$

it compares parameter values for the data that were actually observed.

## Deriving the estimator

Recall that the [natural logarithm turns products into sums while preserving
their ordering](../foundations/zipfs-law.qmd#likelihoods-and-logarithms).
Applying it to the likelihood gives the **log likelihood**

$$
\ell(p)=k\log p+(n-k)\log(1-p).
$$

The logarithm is strictly increasing, so the value of $p$ that maximizes $L(p;\mathbf x)$ also maximizes $\ell(p)$. The log transformation turns products into sums and tends to be more stable numerically.

Recall that a [derivative is a local rate of
change](../random-variables-and-distributions/expected-values.qmd#derivatives-as-local-rates-of-change).
Here $\partial\ell(p)/\partial p$ is the local slope of the log likelihood as
we vary $p$; this likelihood derivative is called the **score**. An
**interior point** has $0<p<1$, so we can consider small changes in either
direction without leaving the parameter space. An interior point at which the
score is zero is called a [**stationary
point**](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/StationaryPoint.html): the log
likelihood is locally flat there.

Differentiate and set the score to zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial p}
&=\frac{k}{p}-\frac{n-k}{1-p}=0,\\
k(1-p)&=(n-k)p,\\
\widehat p_{\mathrm{MLE}}&=\frac{k}{n}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The **second derivative** records how the first derivative, or slope, changes
as $p$ changes. Here it is

$$
\frac{\partial^2\ell}{\partial p^2}
=-\frac{k}{p^2}-\frac{n-k}{(1-p)^2},
$$

and it is negative throughout the interior whenever both outcomes occur. Thus
the slope decreases as $p$ moves from left to right: it is positive before the
stationary point and negative after it. The stationary point is therefore the
unique interior maximum.

There are two boundary cases. If $k=0$, the likelihood is maximized at $\widehat p=0$; if $k=n$, it is maximized at $\widehat p=1$. The derivative calculation above assumes $0<k<n$, while the general estimator $\widehat \mathbb{P}(\mathbf X)=K(\mathbf X)/n$ covers all three cases. Before observation, $\widehat \mathbb{P}(\mathbf X)$ is random. After observing $K(\mathbf x)=k$, $\widehat p=k/n$ is the realized estimate. The [estimator page](properties-of-estimators.qmd#estimators-are-random-variables) develops this random-rule versus realized-value distinction in full.

## Fitting the BOUN labels

```{r}
#| label: fit-ud-bernoulli-mle
library(ggplot2)

pronouns <- read.csv(
  "data/ud-turkish-boun/personal-pronoun-cases.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
n <- nrow(pronouns)
k <- sum(pronouns$accusative)
p_hat <- k / n

negative_log_likelihood <- function(p) {
  if (p <= 0 || p >= 1) return(Inf)
  -(k * log(p) + (n - k) * log1p(-p))
}

p_numerical <- optimize(
  negative_log_likelihood,
  interval = c(1e-8, 1 - 1e-8), # dqr-allow: scale-boundary
  tol = .Machine$double.eps^0.5
)$minimum

likelihood_grid <- data.frame(p = seq(0.12, 0.29, length.out = 500L))
likelihood_grid$log_likelihood <- with(
  likelihood_grid,
  k * log(p) + (n - k) * log1p(-p)
)
likelihood_grid$relative_log_likelihood <-
  likelihood_grid$log_likelihood - max(likelihood_grid$log_likelihood)

stopifnot(abs(p_numerical - p_hat) < 1e-7)

data.frame(
  tokens = n,
  accusative_tokens = k,
  analytic_mle = p_hat,
  numerical_mle = p_numerical
)
```

The analytic and numerical estimates agree at $\widehat p=$ `r sprintf("%.6f", p_hat)`.

The formula-to-code bridge is direct. `k * log(p) + (n - k) * log1p(-p)` evaluates $\ell(p)$, the leading minus sign makes a minimizer solve the maximization problem, and `optimize()` searches the interior interval. The assertion compares this numerical solution with the analytic value `k / n`.

```{r}
#| label: plot-ud-bernoulli-likelihood
#| fig-cap: "Relative Bernoulli log likelihood for the BOUN accusative labels. The vertical line marks the maximum."
ggplot(likelihood_grid, aes(p, relative_log_likelihood)) +
  geom_line(color = "grey25", linewidth = 0.85) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = p_hat, color = "#8B1A1A", linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Shared accusative probability", y = "Log likelihood relative to maximum") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

This estimate maximizes the likelihood within a model that treats token indicators as IID. It does not establish that the model is adequate, remove register variation, or generalize the finite treebank to all Turkish usage.

## Recap and forward link

1. Probability varies over possible data at fixed $p$; likelihood varies over candidate $p$ values for fixed observed data.
2. Logging preserves the maximizer and turns the Bernoulli product into a sum.
3. The score equation gives $K/n$ in the interior, with zero and one as boundary solutions.
4. Numerical optimization checks the derivation; it does not supply additional evidence for the IID model.

The [Poisson maximum-likelihood page](poisson-maximum-likelihood.qmd#deriving-the-poisson-estimator) applies the same logic to sentence-level counts.

## Check your understanding

1. Why can a likelihood fail to sum or integrate to one over parameter values?
2. Which statistic of the binary data appears in the likelihood after terms are collected?
3. How does the second derivative establish that the stationary point is a maximum?
4. Which part of the treebank structure is absent from this likelihood?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. A likelihood is a function of the parameter for fixed observed data; it is not required to normalize over parameter values. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. Only the number of successes, $k=\sum_i x_i$, appears after the Bernoulli terms are collected. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. The second derivative is negative for every interior $p$ when both outcomes occur, so the stationary point is the unique maximum. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. The likelihood omits the nesting of tokens within sentences and registers, as well as any document structure. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
